correctness.rationale: In any n-vertex simplex, \(n-1\) equal-weight edge points averaging to its centroid must contribute \((n-1)/n\) to each vertex barycentric coordinate. This excludes all vertices. A disconnected support multigraph would have a component with k vertices containing \(r=k(n-1)/n\) selected points; coprimality forces a contradiction for \(1\le k<n\). Thus the support is a spanning tree. Summing coordinates across each cut proves the unique \((n-k)/n\) and \(k/n\) edge coefficients; the partition of neighbor components proves the converse. Every tree gives a distinct configuration, counted by Cayley. For a regular simplex, the standard Gram realization gives squared displacement of each edge point; sum \(k(n-k)\) over tree cuts equals the Wiener index. The centering identity converts radial inertia to all-pairs squared-distance energy. Elementary sharp path/star Wiener bounds, with equality, yield the displayed energy interval. The actual included verifier reconstructs and checks the formulas using exact rational arithmetic, exhaustive \(3\le n\le6\) and finite additional samples; the general proof is analytic.
risks: The all-dimensional assertion is mathematical rather than certified by bounded enumeration.
Wiener extremal results are classical external ingredients but their needed special case and equalities are proved in full.

value.rationale: Equal-mass edge placements that balance a simplex at its vertex centroid are a canonical finite-dimensional instance of the published skeleton barycenter problem. Exact classification for every dimension turns a general existence assertion into a constructive discrete parameterization of all configurations: the number is exactly \(n^{n-2}\), and each point coordinate is the size of a tree-cut component. The regular simplex supplies a natural invariant, summed squared pairwise separation of the balancing masses, and its exact reduction to the Wiener index supplies sharp geometrically meaningful rigidity, with paths and stars at the two ends. This is a full natural family classification and a nontrivial geometry/graph metric bridge; it is not a minor numeric example or renaming of Cayley alone.
risks: The metric identity requires regular simplices and does not directly optimize arbitrary simplex Euclidean dispersion.
